title: Hungry, Not Starving
description: How long you last without food, what calories do, and why water and warmth come first
tryIt: For one ordinary day, add up the calories on the labels of everything you eat and compare the total with the NHS guide of about 2,000 to 2,500 kcal.

concepts.title: How it works: fuel, reserves and priorities
concepts.contentHtml:
Day three. Your stomach is growling like a bear in a cave, the river is full of fish that refuse to cooperate, and you are eyeing your leather belt with real interest. Take a breath. You are hungry, which is miserable, but you are a very long way from starving.

Food is fuel. The US Army's survival manual, FM 21-76, calls calories a measure of heat and potential energy, and says the average person needs 2,000 calories per day to function at a minimum level.1 The NHS gives a guide of about 2,500 kcal a day for an average man and 2,000 for an average woman.2 When you eat less than you burn, the NHS explains, your body uses its stored fat for energy.3 A healthy, well-fed adult can fast totally for 48 to 72 hours before ketosis sets in,4 and if the shortfall goes on long enough, the Army manual warns, the body starts consuming its own tissue for energy.

So how long have you got? A study of hunger strikes in the Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law puts death at between 6 and 10 weeks of total fasting,5 for someone still drinking water. The same paper notes that the body cannot survive more than a few days without water.6 That gap, days against weeks, is why food sits above water and shelter on the priorities ladder: you climb to it only once the lower rungs are safe. The Army manual turns to wild plants only after you have solved the problems of finding water, shelter and animal food.

Food still matters long before it becomes fatal. The manual says that without food your mental and physical capabilities will deteriorate rapidly, and that dehydration and lack of food and rest predispose a survivor to hypothermia. A hungry body is a colder, clumsier, more careless body. The aim of this skill is not a feast: it is steady fuel, gathered for less energy than it gives back.

concepts.title: In the field: spend calories to win calories
concepts.contentHtml:
Every trip to the river costs energy. The trick in the first month is to spend as little as possible and to aim it at food that pays you back quickly.

  1. Sort water and shelter first. They keep you alive long enough for food to matter.
  2. If water is scarce, do not eat. The Army manual is blunt: food requires water for digestion, so eating uses water you need for cooling.1
  3. Save your energy. The manual's rule is to conserve sweat, not water: limit sweaty work but keep drinking. A fire helps too, because hot food saves the calories your body would spend making heat.2
  4. Go for easy, plentiful food first. The manual's advice is to seek insects, crustaceans, molluscs, fish and reptiles to satisfy your immediate hunger while you prepare slower methods.3
  5. Eat little and often. Big helpings of plant food on an empty stomach can cause diarrhoea, nausea or cramps, even with familiar foods such as green apples and wild onions.
  6. Keep a log. Write down everything you eat and when. If you fall ill, it tells you, and anyone treating you, what to suspect.
Safety The best meal in any survival story is a rescue, so signal and stay findable before you go foraging. Shellfish need special care: the manual warns never to eat shellfish that are not covered by water at high tide,4 and that mussels may be poisonous in tropical zones during the summer. Cook everything you can.

concepts.title: Myth check: how long can you really last?
concepts.contentHtml:
Hunger lies to you. Two popular beliefs help it lie louder.

Myth Without food you will be dead within a few days.
Reality Water is the few-days problem. For someone who keeps drinking, death from total fasting comes at between 6 and 10 weeks, and the Army manual says you can live several weeks without food.1 Hunger feels like an emergency on day two; it is not one yet.
Myth If you are short of water, eat something to keep your strength up.
Reality Digesting food uses water. The manual's rule when water is scarce is simply not to eat, because the water spent on digestion is water you need to stay cool.

Wait, really? Weeks of survival is not the same as weeks of feeling fine. From November 1944 to late October 1945, the physiologist Ancel Keys ran a starvation experiment at the University of Minnesota with thirty-six young male volunteers,2 all conscientious objectors. The point was not starvation itself but learning how to re-feed millions of war victims. For six months the men lived on a bland diet of the kind war victims ate (macaroni, turnips, weak soup, potatoes and rutabaga) while walking twenty-two miles a week. Most lost 24 per cent of their weight, and their emotional health suffered.3 The answer turned out to be simple: more calories.4 Even the Army manual warns that you must not count on going for days without food, as some sources suggest.

title: Hook, Line and Weir
description: The oldest fish hooks, making a gorge and line, where fish lie, and weirs in history
tryIt: On a riverbank walk, find three places a fish could rest out of the current: an eddy behind a rock, a deep pool and a spot under overhanging branches.

concepts.title: How it works: 23,000 years of hooks
concepts.contentHtml:
You are sitting on a rock above a river full of fish, armed with a bootlace, a safety pin and a growing sense of injustice. The good news: people have been solving exactly this problem for more than twenty thousand years.

Fish are worth the effort. The Army manual calls them a good source of protein and fat, usually more abundant than mammals, and adds that the ways to get them are silent.1 The oldest proof that people made tackle for them comes from islands in the western Pacific. In Sakitari Cave on Okinawa, Japan, a team led by Masaki Fujita found what they describe as the world's oldest fishhook, in a layer dated to 23,000 years ago.2 It is a single-piece hook made by splitting and grinding the flat base of a3 Trochus sea-snail shell, and the team also found an unfinished one.

Further south, at Jerimalai shelter in East Timor, Sue O'Connor, Rintaro Ono and Chris Clarkson reported fish remains dating to 42,000 years ago, including deep-sea species such as tuna, together with what was then the earliest definite evidence for fishhook manufacture in the world.4 Those Timor shell hooks date to roughly 23,000 to 16,000 years ago, so the Okinawa find is comparable or older.5 Together they show that hook technology had spread from the islands of Wallacea north to the edge of the western Pacific by the coldest part of the last Ice Age.

Hooks are only one answer. The Army manual's improvised hooks use pins, needles, wire, small nails, wood, bone, thorns, flint, seashell or tortoise shell, and its simplest device has no bend at all: the gorge, a small shaft sharp at both ends and tied at a notch in the middle.6 Bait it lengthwise, and when the fish swallows the bait, it swallows the gorge too. By Roman times, fishers in Egypt were using barbed hooks of copper alloy.

concepts.title: In the field: reading water and rigging a line
concepts.contentHtml:
Fish are not spread evenly through a river. They wait where food comes to them and the current does not wear them out. Learn to see those places and half the work is done.

  1. Read the water. In a heavy current, fish rest where there is an eddy, such as near rocks.1 They also gather in deep pools, under overhanging brush, and around sunken logs and weed that give them shelter.
  2. Pick your moment. The Army manual says fish tend to feed heavily before a storm, and that light often attracts fish at night.2
  3. Make a gorge or hook. For a lashed hook, the manual suggests a hardwood shank about 2.5 centimetres long and 6 millimetres thick,3 notched at one end, with a point of bone, wire or nail tied into the notch.
  4. Rig a line. Thin cord from the cordage skill works, or the inner strands of paracord.
  5. Bait and wait. Thread bait lengthwise along a gorge and give the fish time to swallow it before you pull.
  6. Deal with the catch fast. Gut any fish longer than 10 centimetres, and cook all freshwater fish to kill parasites.4
Safety Check the fishing rules first. In England and Wales you need a rod fishing licence to fish for freshwater fish with a rod and line, even on private land,5 plus permission from the landowner, and you must follow national and local byelaws. The fine for fishing without a licence can reach £2,500.6 Scotland, Northern Ireland and other countries have their own rules, so check what methods are allowed before you try anything but a rod. Catfish spines can cause painful puncture wounds that quickly become infected.

concepts.title: Myth check: storms, bone hooks and fish fences
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Fish bite best after a storm, when the river is churned up.
Reality The Army manual says the opposite: fish tend to feed heavily before a storm and are not likely to feed after one, when the water is muddy and swollen.1
Myth The world's oldest fish hooks are 42,000-year-old bone hooks from Timor.
Reality Some news stories in 2011 said so,2 but the 42,000-year date belongs to the fish bones at Jerimalai.3 The hooks there are shell, about 23,000 to 16,000 years old. Sue O'Connor has suggested that the tuna may have been caught in the deep channel just off the coast.4

Wait, really? Some of the cleverest fishing gear never needed a hook. A weir is a fence across a river or shore that steers fish into a pen. On the Pacific coast of North America, Coast Salish weirs and traps penned fish alive behind a barrier, so fishers could release female salmon and harvest the males,5 keeping the run healthy. That power cut both ways: used carelessly, a weir could destroy a salmon run by blocking the way to the spawning grounds, so only chiefs, weir specialists and shamans with the right knowledge built and ran them.6 At Ahnkuti on the Oregon coast, the remains of a 2,200-year-old intertidal fish weir survive.7 The Army manual's tidal trap uses the same trick: fish come inshore with the rising tide, so you pick the spot at high tide and build at low tide.8

title: Traps: History and Principle
description: Desert kites and drive lanes, how a trap really works, and why snares are now banned in many places
tryIt: On a walk at dawn or dusk, find an animal run or trail, look for tracks, droppings or nibbled plants, and photograph what you find without disturbing it.

concepts.title: How it works: funnels, from desert kites to snares
concepts.contentHtml:
A rabbit runs past your shelter every evening at dusk, and you have started to take it personally. Before you do anything about it, it is worth knowing how trapping works, how old it is, and why much of it is now illegal.

Trapping is one of humanity's oldest technologies. In the deserts of Jordan and Saudi Arabia, archaeologists have mapped desert kites: giant traps built of stone walls, the oldest dated to at least 9,000 years ago.1 Each has driving lines from hundreds of metres to 5 kilometres long, converging on an enclosure about a hectare across that is ringed by pits up to 4 metres deep, where animals were trapped.2 In 2023 a team led by Rémy Crassard described stones engraved with plans of nearby kites, so precise that they rank as the oldest known plans drawn to scale.3

The principle never changed: a trap is a funnel plus a place the animal cannot leave. The Army manual calls it channelization: build a funnel-shaped barrier from the sides of a trail towards the trap, narrowest nearest the trap, so that as the animal arrives it cannot turn left or right. The manual also explains why trapping appealed to soldiers: several well-placed traps have the potential to catch much more game than a hunter with a rifle, and they keep working while you are elsewhere.

That is also the problem. A trap holds whatever walks into it until someone comes back, and the manual itself admits there are no catch-all traps you can set for all animals. What you catch is decided by where you put the funnel, not by what you hoped for.

concepts.title: In the field: reading sign, not setting snares
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is the honest field skill: learning where animals go. It is the part of trapping that harms nothing, and it teaches you more about a place than any snare.

  1. Go at dawn or dusk. Grazing animals such as deer are usually never far from water and usually drink at dawn and dusk.1
  2. Find the paths. A trail shows signs of several species and is fairly distinct; a run is smaller, fainter and used by one species.
  3. Read the sign. Look for tracks, droppings, chewed or rubbed vegetation, nesting or roosting sites, and feeding and watering areas.
  4. Follow the network. Animals have bedding areas, waterholes and feeding areas with trails between them, and converging game trails often lead to water.2
  5. Stay downwind and light-footed. Nearly all mammals depend on smell even more than on sight, and freshly cut plants bleed sap whose smell alarms them.
  6. Leave only footprints. Photograph or sketch what you find and move on.
Safety Trapping law varies and is getting stricter. Scotland's Wildlife Management and Muirburn (Scotland) Act 2024 bans snares, except snares operated by hand,3 and bans glue traps unless authorised.4 Wales has banned snares, other cable restraints and glue traps.5 In England self-locking snares are illegal and any snare must be inspected at least once every day.6 Elsewhere the rules and licences vary, so find out first. Never set a trap just to see whether it works.

concepts.title: Myth check: snares, perfect traps and a wall under the sea
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A snare is a quick, clean way to catch a meal.
Reality Lawmakers disagree. English law bans self-locking snares outright,1 and Scotland and Wales have now banned almost all snaring. A wire loop cannot tell a rabbit from a pet, and it holds whatever it catches until someone returns.
Myth Build a good enough trap and it will catch something anywhere.
Reality The Army manual says you may construct a perfect snare, but it will not catch anything if haphazardly placed in the woods. Placement on real signs of passage matters far more than craftsmanship.

Wait, really? In 2024 a German team led by Jacob Geersen reported a stone wall lying 21 metres under the Baltic Sea in the Bay of Mecklenburg. The Blinkerwall is made of 1,673 stones, mostly less than a metre high, placed side by side for 971 metres2 beside the drowned shoreline of an old lake. The researchers think hunter-gatherers built it after the ice sheet retreated, to drive reindeer,3 using the animals' habit of being drawn to straight lines,4 and it may be the oldest human-made megastructure in Europe.5 A funnel, once again, just a very big one.

title: Forage by Rules
description: Why plants poison, why mushrooms are a firm no, insects as food, and why the edibility test fails
tryIt: In a garden or park, photograph five wild plants and identify them later with a field guide, without picking or tasting any of them.

concepts.title: How it works: why plants and fungi poison
concepts.contentHtml:
There is a bush loaded with fat purple berries, a ring of pale mushrooms that look just like the ones from the shop, and a small voice in your head asking how bad it could really be. This lesson is that voice's worst nightmare.

Plants poison in three ways, the Army manual explains: when they are eaten, when they touch the skin, or when they are absorbed or breathed in. How dangerous a plant is depends on the dose, on how much toxin that particular plant made in its growing conditions, and on the person eating it. Some familiar plants have both edible and poisonous parts: potatoes and tomatoes are common foods, but their green parts are poisonous.1 Others are lethal lookalikes. Poison hemlock has killed people who mistook it for its relatives, wild carrots and wild parsnips. Its cousin water hemlock has a reputation, one ethnobotanist wrote, as the most poisonous plant in the North Temperate Zone;2 its toxin can cause seizures and vomiting within 60 minutes of eating it, frequently leading to death.3

Fungi are worse, because the deadliest ones act slowly. The death cap, Amanita phalloides, is responsible for most deaths after eating foraged mushrooms worldwide.4 Its amatoxins stop cells making proteins, and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) notes that they are heat stable and are not inactivated by cooking.5 A lethal dose can be as low as 0.1 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, and a single mushroom can contain up to 15 milligrams.6

In December 2016, California's poison control system logged fourteen death cap poisonings among people who had eaten foraged mushrooms. Three needed liver transplants, and a child was left with permanent neurological damage.7 The CDC's conclusion is short: inexperienced foragers should be strongly discouraged from eating any wild mushrooms.8

concepts.title: In the field: the forager's rules
concepts.contentHtml:
This course will never tell you which wild plant to eat, because a screen cannot see the plant in your hand. What it can give you are rules that keep you alive while you learn properly, from a local expert, with the plant in front of you both.

  1. Mushrooms: no. Not unless an experienced mycologist has examined the actual specimen. The Army manual is flat: do not eat mushrooms in a survival situation.
  2. Plants: only with certainty. Eat only plants you can positively identify and know are safe.
  3. Know the red flags. The manual says to avoid unknown plants with milky or discoloured sap; beans, bulbs or seeds inside pods; a bitter or soapy taste; spines, fine hairs or thorns; carrot- or parsley-like leaves; an almond scent; grain heads with dark spurs; or three-leaved growth. These rules will rule out some good plants, and that is the point.
  4. Turn to insects. Look in rotting logs for ants, termites, beetles and grubs, and under stones and boards.1
  5. Cook hard-shelled insects. Beetles and grasshoppers can carry parasites, so cook them and remove wings and barbed legs.2 Avoid insects that sting or bite, hairy or brightly coloured ones, caterpillars and anything with a strong smell,3 plus spiders, ticks, flies and mosquitoes.
  6. Skip the roadside. Plants near houses or roads may have been sprayed with pesticides, and fruit that is starting to spoil can carry fungal toxins.
Safety If someone may have eaten a poisonous plant or fungus, call emergency services at once. Early death cap poisoning can look like a stomach bug,4 so tell doctors about any wild food. In one of the 2016 California cases, a leftover uncooked mushroom let a mycologist name the culprit,5 so keep a sample if you can. Allergies to eating insects are scarce but do exist.6

concepts.title: Myth check: the edibility test and other folk rules
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The universal edibility test will tell you whether any plant is safe to eat.
Reality The test, printed in the Army manual and repeated widely, has you touch a piece to your lip, chew it, swallow a little and wait 8 hours before eating more.1 But a death cap's silent phase lasts 6 to 24 hours,2 and water hemlock can bring seizures within the hour. The test can catch a plant that burns or stings; it cannot catch a slow killer or a tiny lethal dose. The manual itself bars mushrooms (there is no room for experimentation) and warns that each part of a plant requires more than 24 hours to test.
Myth If animals eat it, or if you boil it, it is safe.
Reality Some animals can eat plants that are poisonous to humans:3 water birds eat water hemlock fruits without ill effect.4 Boiling removes many poisons, but not all,5 and death cap toxins survive cooking.

Wait, really? Even famous numbers get tested. FAO's landmark 2013 report on edible insects estimated that insects form part of the traditional diets of at least 2 billion people,6 from fried locusts and beetles in Thailand to the mopane caterpillars of southern Africa, and found more than 1,900 species used as food.7 In 2022 the report's own lead author, Arnold van Huis, and his colleagues concluded that the 2 billion figure must be an overestimation,8 though several hundred million could be possible.9 Insects remain a real food, just a less universal one than the headlines said.

title: Keeping Food
description: Drying, smoking and salting, how water activity starves microbes, and dodging food poisoning
tryIt: Weigh some thin apple slices, dry them on a rack in a warm, airy place or a low oven, then weigh them again to see how much water you removed.

concepts.title: How it works: starving the microbes
concepts.contentHtml:
Good news: the fish trap worked. Bad news: you have nine fish, one stomach and a hot afternoon. The Army manual warns that fish spoils quickly after death, especially on a hot day,1 so the race is on.

Spoilage is microbes eating your food before you do, and like you they need water. Food scientists measure how available a food's water is as water activity: the ratio of the food's vapour pressure to that of pure water, so a water activity of 0.80 means 80 per cent of pure water's.2 The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) notes that most foods sit above 0.95, which is plenty for bacteria, yeasts and moulds.3 Reduce the available moisture and growth stops. The botulism bacterium, Clostridium botulinum, needs at least about 0.93,4 and the FDA treats foods held at 0.85 or below as outside its strict canning regulations.5

There are two ways down the scale. Drying removes water outright. Salting ties it up, because a salt or sugar solution has a lower vapour pressure than pure water.6 Slow smoking dries food as well: properly smoked meat, says the Army manual, looks like a dark, curled, brittle stick. The CDC lists the conditions in which botulism spores grow and make toxin:7 little or no oxygen, low acid, low sugar, low salt, a certain temperature range and a certain amount of water. Every preserving trick takes at least one of those away.

People worked this out long before anyone measured a vapour pressure. Drying is one of the oldest ways of preserving food.8 In southern Africa, where an estimated 9.5 billion mopane caterpillars are harvested every year,9 the caterpillars are degutted, boiled in salted water and sun-dried, and the dried caterpillars last for several months.10

concepts.title: In the field: drying, smoking and salting
concepts.contentHtml:
The Army manual's methods are simple and slow. The whole aim is to get water out, or salt in, before microbes get going.

  1. Clean it fast. Prepare fish as soon as possible after catching it. To smoke fish, cut off the head and remove the backbone.1
  2. Slice thin. For drying, cut meat into strips about 6 millimetres thick, with the grain. For smoking, keep slices no more than 6 centimetres thick.
  3. Dry in sun and wind. Hang strips on a rack in a sunny, airy place, out of reach of animals and covered against blowflies. Properly dried meat is dry and crisp and does not feel cool to the touch.
  4. Or smoke it. Build an enclosure round a small fire: the aim is smoke, not heat. Use hardwood that is somewhat green, never resinous wood, and drape the strips so no piece touches another. Meat smoked overnight lasts about a week; two days of continuous smoking preserves it for 2 to 4 weeks.
  5. Or salt it. Soak meat in brine that covers it completely, or pack it in salt, and wash the salt off before cooking.
  6. Heat it if you can. The US National Center for Home Food Preservation advises bringing home-dried jerky to an internal 160°F (71°C),2 by heating the strips in their marinade before drying or in an oven afterwards.
Safety Botulism is the preserver's nightmare. The CDC names homemade foods that have been improperly canned, preserved or fermented as common sources,3 and every kind of botulism is a medical emergency, so never seal damp fish or meat away from the air. For ordinary food poisoning, the NHS says the most important thing is to drink plenty of fluids;4 call 999 or your local emergency number if someone vomits blood, is confused or not responding as usual, or may have swallowed something poisonous.

concepts.title: Myth check: freezing, cooking and a Viking fish supper
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Freezing kills the germs in meat.
Reality Freezing will not eliminate bacteria from meat,1 warns the US National Center for Home Food Preservation, and the Army manual agrees that freezing is not a means of preparing meat: you must still cook it. Long, deep freezing does kill the trichinella parasite in wild game, at 0°F (about minus 18°C) for at least 30 days, for pieces 6 inches thick or less.2
Myth If fish smells a bit off, just cook it longer.
Reality Cooking does not ensure that spoiled fish will be edible.3 The manual's warning signs are sunken eyes, an odd smell, a suspicious colour (gills should be red to pink), flesh that keeps a dent when pressed, a slimy body and a sharp or peppery taste. Spoiled fish can cause diarrhoea, vomiting, itching and even paralysis, with symptoms appearing one to six hours after eating.4

Wait, really? Some preserved food travelled astonishing distances. In Lofoten, in Arctic Norway, cod arrive to spawn just when the weather is right for freeze-drying them in the open air without the use of expensive salt,5 and the dried stockfish became a great medieval export. In 2017 a team led by Bastiaan Star read the DNA of cod bones from Haithabu, a Viking Age town in northern Germany, and traced them to the North East Arctic cod population that still supports the Lofoten fishery.6 Somebody's supper had been dried in the Arctic and carried all the way to the Baltic.7
